data.title: The mythology of death among the Slavs and other peoples
data.excerpt: With the author's permission we present the full text of Katarína Marčeková's study of how the Slavs and neighbouring peoples imagined death and the afterlife. It follows the chthonic god Veles, the Germanic goddess Hel and the Celtic islands in the ocean, and shows how much of the Slavic picture has to be reconstructed from language alone.

children.text: With the author's permission we present the full text of this interesting scholarly article by Katarína Marčeková.

The phenomenon of death is very closely bound up with the religious ideas of any given people. It is therefore important to emphasise, to describe and to reconstruct the world of religious ideas relating not only to the ritual of death.

The world of Slavic religious ideas was a world in which Germanic, Celtic and Graeco-Roman ideas intermingled with the original religious ideas of the Slavs. We are unable to make out their core, because after arriving in new territories they absorbed the ideas current in that territory.

Most of the gods of this milieu whose sphere of action included death and the underworld were of a chthonic character. From the Celtic milieu we know several gods with this function: Aedmac Lir, Aericura, Arianrhod.1 There were likewise several Graeco-Roman deities2, but the greatest interest will be aroused by Hades/Pluto, where a parallel can be drawn with the Slavic god Veles, and by the Germanic goddess Hel.

was the Slavic god of fertility and the protector of cattle, crops, property and prosperity, and also the god of the underworld. He was worshipped by the Eastern Slavs, with centres in Kiev and Rostov. He was probably a universal god, as is shown by the surviving personal and place names and by relics in folk dialect. His cult is recorded by sources such as the Povesti vremennych let (the Tale of Bygone Years), the Slovo o pluku Igorovom (the Tale of Igor's Campaign) and the Legend of St Vladimir from as early as the 10th century. His worship, however, is also placed in an earlier period. After the consolidation of Christianity he was identified with the devil, or rather with the fiend, as were most of the deities of the Slavic pantheon. His attributes of bull's horns and phallic symbols probably also contributed to this easier degradation.3 If we accept the thesis of his function as god of the underworld, the question arises how the god of cattle and property could have become the probable god of the underworld. The answer may perhaps be found in a comparison with the Greek Hades. He is among the oldest Greek gods. He is regarded as the chthonic counterpart of the god Zeus. He is the lord of the realm of the dead and at the same time also the god of wealth (property), because all the precious metals and stones are stored in the earth.4 In view of the contacts of this territory with the classical one, a transfer of ideas from the ancient world to here may be assumed. But a more reliable answer is probably that the reports of Veles as god of the underworld come from the classical cultural sphere, and so a parallel between him and Hades may have manifested itself in the understanding. From the point of view of linguistics, the closest parallels to Veles as god of the underworld are in the Baltic cultural sphere, in both aspects: both as the god of cattle – Veles, Velinas – and as the ruler of the underworld – véles (the souls of the dead), Velionis (deus animarum), Vels (the Latvian god of death), vela (the kingdom of the dead), Velinas, Velnias, Vels (the devil). In Czech, too, the name “veles” was used as a synonym for the devil, the fiend.5

The Germanic goddess Hel is likewise a chthonic goddess of the underworld. Her domain is also called Hel. There she rules over all the dead with the exception of those fallen in battle, whom the valkyries escort to Valhalla. One half of her body is white and the other half black6, by which she expresses the indivisible dualism of life and death. She rules in Niflheim over nine worlds, which is the dwelling of those who will be sent to her, that is, of those who die of old age or of disease.7 We do not know the ideas about the Slavic afterlife. We can only attempt to demonstrate two other sets of ideas, the Celtic and the Germanic, for which we have sufficient written sources, and hope that the Slavic ideas shared at least a few features with them.
From the numerous reports of classical authors we may conclude that the

believed in the immortality of the soul. Caesar states in his Commentaries that according to druidic teaching the soul does not perish but after death passes from one into another.8 This does present us with a kind of form of reincarnation of the soul, but we know nothing more about it. Diodorus Siculus in his

likewise says that “human souls are immortal and after a certain number of years return into another body”.9 It generally holds that, according to the ideas of the Romans, the Celts' belief in an afterlife and in a sojourn in the land of eternal happiness and youth gave them courage in battle and freed them from the fear of death. In presenting Celtic eschatological ideas, however, several problems arise, the most important of which are the terms and the placing of a particular idea within some framework. This question is dealt with in her contribution by Tatiana Podolinská, who presents these ideas in such a way that death is for a Celt merely the middle of a long life. We cannot say, however, even whether it is a linear or a cyclical life and conception. Celtic teaching is generally characterised by the idea of the transmigration of the soul and the idea of the immortality of the soul, whereby it is essential that it is a bodily existence of the soul after death. Their soul therefore departs in (another) body to another world, and the possibility of a renewed return to this world is not excluded.10 The belief in the afterlife of the soul is connected with the idea of the place where this soul dwells. One way of reaching this place was a journey by boat (these often belonged directly to beings from the otherworld), sometimes a glass boat without oars or sails, when the boat itself knew the way.

The otherworld was located geographically to the west of the Atlantic and had the form of an island in the middle of the ocean. It was the seat of people as well as of gods. It could be reached not only by sailing across the sea but also by means of mental transfer. The names varied, but all had one feature in common: they described something that was attainable only with difficulty in the ordinary life of the Celts and from which they promised themselves a sweet and wholly undisturbed life: Tir mBeo (the land of the living), Tir na mBan (the land of women), Tir na nOg (the land of the young), Tir Sorcha (the land of light), Mag Mor (the great land), Mag Meld (the land of delights). Their geographical localisation is relatively simple: according to Plutarch, who cites the older source Demetrius, to the west of Britain there are islands bearing the names of gods and kings.11
It was precisely wandering through unknown places that allowed a specialised genre to arise in Irish literature – the

The two best known are: The Voyage of Bran and The Sea Voyage of Máel Dúin's Boat. In general both these works, chiefly The Voyage of Bran, are regarded as an allegorical journey of the soul: “A woman comes to Bran with a branch that she has brought from the otherworld. She urges him to set out for this place. She also foretells to him the birth of Christ, as born of a virgin without beginning or end. Bran lets himself be persuaded and with his 26 companions crosses the Plain of Delight (a paradise where there is no sin) and arrives at the Island of Joy. Then he reaches the Island of Women as a place of wanton delights. One of the travellers – Nechtáin – longs for home and the queen of the island lets them all depart. Before that, however, she warns them on no account to step onto the land. When they do return, Nechtáin disobeys and steps onto the land; at that moment he turns to ash. Bran introduces himself and the people answer that they do not know him, but that The Voyage of Bran is one of their oldest tales. Bran understands that he has indeed returned home, but several centuries later; he therefore recounts his adventures to them and they sail back out to the open sea.” From this story it follows that it is never possible to return completely from the otherworld. In later stories the otherworld moved from the sea to dry land. The places of entry were then, for example, in caves, on hills, at springs and lakes. The time when the boundaries between the world of the living and the world of the dead were almost erased was the time of the feast of Samhain.12 The dead came to their living relatives to warm themselves at the fire and to eat the food of mortals. At that time the living too could enter the places inhabited by the dead and set out along the roads of the otherworld. Not all of them, however, were led by friendly motives. Some of the dead came to harm people. Various anti-vampire measures were meant to prevent these unwanted returns.

of Snorri Sturluson. Although with the Edda there is a risk of an attempt by the Christian organisation to take control of the mythological world, the individual phenomena extracted from the literary context probably do render a narrative mythological system. The fate of people is decided by three maidens, the norns Urd (Fate), Verdandi (Constancy) and Skuld (Duty), who rule over human destinies.13 The dead have several worlds as their destination. Those who have the true faith will dwell in a place called Gimlé or Víngolf, while the wicked will go to Hel and from there to Niflhel, that is, deep down into the ninth world.14 It is precisely in this passage that Christian cosmology manifests itself perhaps most clearly. Gimlé/Víngolf is the Nordic paradise intended for people with the “true faith”. Its hall surpasses all the others in beauty and shines brighter than the sun. It is situated as far up as the third heaven: Vídbláin, Andlang.15 The cosmology of Christianity is reflected in the assumption that the heaven of the Germanic peoples had several parts situated one above the other. Hel/Níflhel/Níflheim are probably names used in parallel for one and the same place. Hel is derived from the name of the goddess who rules in this place. Niflheim is a land of shades, perhaps similar to the land of shades in Virgil's Aeneid. Both heaven and the underworld are divided in a similar way to the division of the Christian heaven and hell into several levels.16 In the Edda this division is best visible in the description of the events after Ragnarök.17 There is yet another place intended for the caste of warriors who died on the battlefield. “Fólkvang se zvedům, kde Freyja poroučí, kdo zasadne v síni. Polovinu padlých pokaždé si vyvolí, druhou si odvádí Ódin.”18 (quoted here in the Czech translation of the Edda; in English: Fólkvangr is where Freyja decides who shall be seated in the hall; half of the slain she chooses every time, the other half Odin takes away.) The dead intended for Odin are chosen by the valkyries, women warriors whose name means “those who choose the slain”. They decide who will win and who will fall.19 They then lead the slain away to Valhalla, handing over half of them to the goddess Freyja. Valhalla is similar to the heavenly Jerusalem; here too everyone has an allotted place, only one has to get there by one's merits. In the Edda these are the merits of those fallen in battle.
is not easy to reconstruct. The greatest possibilities are offered to us by the use of linguistics to decipher the terms. The word
is a word of Gothic origin that denotes the souls of the dead or the otherworld. The root of the word may, however, equally come from the Graeco-Latin term

– as a boat serving to ferry the dead.20 According to Dušan Čaplovič, the idea of life beyond the grave was also connected with the idea of life beyond the sea or in a deep underworld.21 The idea of underworld deities, however, was not unknown to them (it may also be suggested by the lower band of the Zbruch idol) and need not be exclusively a product of the classification of Christianity. The dualistic existence of good and evil is also attested by the cosmogonic version of the

Their otherworld was not divided according to merits, according to an ethical scale of values. Even terms such as “raj” (paradise) and “ad” (hell) speak of the otherworld in general and do not specify it as a particular place only for one category of people. Although the word
– hell is undoubtedly of Slavic origin, it need not automatically indicate hell according to Christian ideas. Originally it is similar to a translation of the Latin word

– pitch. The Slavs might have imagined the otherworld as a place where wicked people were burnt with pitch/fire and named the whole place hell accordingly. This idea, however, is not original. The place of punishment is a Christian application. The Slavs knew hell only from the time when they were already acquainted with Christianity, and they derived its name from a certain property of it discussed by Christianity.23 The Slavic otherworld is a world of shades, a place to which all come without distinction. The manner of their “life” in the otherworld was, however, qualitatively different depending on the care shown to them by the survivors, on the funeral rite performed and on the manner of death. Those who were buried in accordance with the rite led a contented life. Those, however, who left the world by a violent death or were not properly buried wandered between this world and the otherworld and returned to the world of people. These apparitions, the “nave”, were later interpreted as demons of evil, as devils. We can therefore find the Christian devil also in the Slavic belief in the “mory, nave”, in apparitions and spectres, vampires and revenants, which had the power to harm the living and to take revenge on them.24 Heaven was the counterpart of the earth. The expression corresponds to the Old Indian

and represents the sky with clouds. It is therefore not a place of reward for the righteous as in Christianity. There are, however, also later ideas already qualitatively influenced by Christianity. Heaven blazes like fire, in which God is hidden; the angels and saints live in the visible heaven, where only the souls of the dead can come. Its vault touches the earth and reaches down to the bottom of the sea.25 Most of the terms connected with terminology such as god, faith or saint are of Iranian origin, and thus point to Slavic-Iranian cultural ties and to a share in Slavic ethnogenesis. “Div, diva, divý” is for the Slavs a nature spirit, to which correspond the Old Indian “deva”, the Iranian “div, daeva”, the Latin “divus, deus, dea” and the Lithuanian “dévas”.26 Their funeral rite, however, is different.27 The Slavs thus took over the terminology from the Iranian cultural sphere, but the funeral rite from the Indo-European one. It is not only Slavic religion that has its roots in a common Indo-European basis. It therefore has features in common with the religious systems of the Indians, Iranians, Greeks, Romans, Germanic peoples, Celts and Balts.28

It is not easy to create and present the original world of Slavic ideas. We can only assume that they had a relatively similar composition to the mythological ideas of other Indo-European peoples. One way of gaining a closer view of their composition is to combine historical and religious-studies research with linguistic research, which may point the way.
